title: The Exposure Map
titleHtml: Map your team's work by AI exposure.
tagline: Walking your team's work through an AI-exposure lens.
description: A 45-minute virtual session for Vanderbilt managers: map your team's recurring work, sort it honestly by AI exposure, and open the team conversation about what changes without fear.
heroLead: AI is already reshaping some of the work your team repeats every week. This session builds your map of which tasks are exposed and which stay human.
objectives: Map your team's recurring work as tasks, separate from the people who hold them
Sort each task honestly by AI exposure: high, partial, or low
Open one team conversation that frames exposure as redesign the team helps write
missionTie: Managers who can map AI exposure and redesign around it keep Exceptional Core Operations exceptional while the tools underneath keep changing.

agenda.d: List the team's recurring work as tasks, because exposure lives in tasks, never in job titles.
Call each task's AI exposure straight: high, partial, or low, without flattery or panic.
Bring the map to your team as a redesign conversation they help write.

manifesto: Write your team's work down as tasks, then sort each one's AI exposure honestly.

sections.headline: Map the work one task at a time.
sections.lead: McKinsey's automation research lands on one steady point: machines take over activities, almost never whole jobs. Start with a list of your team's recurring tasks, the weekly report, the intake queue. Keep people off the page and the picture gets honest fast.

source.label: Jobs lost, jobs gained, McKinsey Global Institute

sections.group: In pairs: name two recurring tasks your team does every week, in task language, no names attached. One pair shares their list.
sections.solo: List five recurring tasks your team does every week, in task language, no names attached.

deeper.title: Write the task like a recipe
deeper.body: A sortable task line has three parts: the output, the rhythm, and the inputs. 'Board report, monthly, from three spreadsheets' sorts in seconds; 'reporting' never will. The entries worth hunting are the invisible ones: work living in one person's head, or the cleanup nobody calls a task. Unlisted tasks are often the most exposed, because nobody has ever looked at them straight.
steps: Rewrite one recurring task as output, rhythm, inputs. If a colleague could picture doing it from your line, it is ready to sort.
Add two invisible tasks to your map: work only one person knows, or cleanup nobody names. Write them in the same format.
Keep the list where you plan your week and add one task line a day until you reach ten.

interaction.context: Map this work by role and the month turns into a quiet argument about whose job is safe. A task on the board puts nobody on trial, so people tell the truth about what the week is made of, and the whole team can study the same work in the open.
interaction.discuss: Name one task your team repeats weekly, in task language: output, rhythm, inputs. What gets easier to say once the name is off it?

card.text: Map the work, never the people. List each recurring task on its own line: what gets produced, how often, from what inputs. A task-level map lets you redesign work without putting anyone's job on trial.

interaction.q: Quick check: which entry belongs on an AI-exposure map?

opts.t: Our data analyst might be replaceable
opts.why: That maps a person, and it poisons every conversation that follows. Exposure belongs to tasks; people hold portfolios of tasks, most of which stay human.

opts.t: Weekly enrollment summary, compiled every Friday from system exports
opts.why: A named task with a rhythm and inputs. Now you can ask how exposed it is and what the hour it frees up should become.

opts.t: The whole front office, since AI changes everything
opts.why: Too big to sort and too vague to redesign. Break it into the tasks the office actually repeats and the map becomes useful.

sections.headline: Give each task one of three calls.
sections.lead: Every task on the map gets one call. High means the task could largely run through AI. Partial means AI helps while a person drives. Low means it stays human. Two habits skew a sort: calling everything exposed, or protecting every task out of loyalty.
sections.group: Breakout pairs: pick one task from your list and call its exposure. Does your partner agree? 90 seconds each way.
sections.solo: Pick one task from your list and call its exposure: high, partial, or low. Write one line on why.

deeper.title: When a task refuses to sort
deeper.body: Some tasks resist a single call because they are bundles. The monthly newsletter is drafting from public content, choosing the lead story, and replying to an upset reader, and each piece sorts differently. When a call feels impossible, split the task into steps and sort the steps; the argument usually dissolves. A sort is also a snapshot: tools improve, so a low call today deserves a fresh look next quarter.
steps: Take the task that was hardest to call. Break it into three or four steps and give each step its own exposure call.
Mark any step touching private information about people. Those stay human, whatever you decide about the rest of the bundle.
Date the sort and set a reminder to rerun it in a quarter.

interaction.intro: Read each task and call its exposure. Notice which detail drives your call: how repetitive the work is, whose data it touches, how much judgment it needs.
interaction.passMsg: You sort straight. High gets a redesign, partial gets a pairing, low gets protected and valued.
interaction.failMsg: Close. The tells: repetitive and rule-based leans high; judgment over internal work leans partial; anything built on trust or private people data stays human.

items.q: Reformatting the same public event listings into the newsletter template every week.
items.why: Repetitive, rule-based, built on public content: green-light work AI handles well. The redesign question is what the freed hours should become.

items.q: Drafting the annual program review, which blends internal data with judgment calls about priorities.
items.why: AI can draft and summarize inside approved VU tools, since the data is internal. The priority calls stay with the person driving.

items.q: Coaching a struggling team member through a rough semester.
items.why: This runs on trust and private knowledge of a person. That is red-light territory for AI and the heart of the job for a manager.

sections.headline: Bring the map to the team.
sections.lead: Share the map early, before rumor fills the gap. Gallup finds people feel far readier for AI when a manager has explained the plan and how it touches their work. Two choices decide how it lands: your opening line and the promise you make.

source.label: Manager support drives employee AI adoption (Gallup)

deeper.title: Keep the map alive after the talk
deeper.body: The opening meeting is the easy part; the promise gets kept in what happens next. Put the map where the team can see and edit it, and treat every task they add as a gift. Then keep the redesign promise visibly the first time it is tested: when the first task moves to a tool, let the team decide in the open what fills the freed hour. One kept promise buys more trust than a season of reassurance.
steps: Draft the two sentences you will open with: the invitation to sort the map together and the freed-hours promise. Say them aloud once before the meeting.
Choose where the shared map will live and add a recurring slot on the team agenda to revisit it.

interaction.intro: Choose your opening line and your promise, then run the meeting. Notice which choices turn the map into shared work and which turn it into a verdict.

opts.t: Leadership wants an AI plan, so I made a list of what could be automated.
opts.coach: Opening with leadership pressure and automation tells the room this is being done to them. Expect quiet nodding in the meeting and loud anxiety after it.

opts.t: AI is coming either way, so let's get ahead of it before it gets ahead of us.
opts.coach: Energetic, and it still frames AI as a threat to outrun. Fear gets attention; it rarely gets honest task lists.

opts.t: Here's a map of our recurring tasks. I want your read on what AI should take off our plates.
opts.coach: Tasks on the table, people invited to sort them. Asking for their read turns the map into shared work instead of a verdict.

opts.t: No promises; we'll see where this goes.
opts.coach: Uncertainty from the manager becomes dread in the team. Without a commitment, every high-exposure task reads as a threat to someone.

opts.t: Nobody's job changes because of this exercise.
opts.coach: Comforting today and hard to keep. Work will change; promising it won't spends your credibility on the wrong sentence.

opts.t: Exposed tasks mean redesign, and the people who do the work help decide what fills the hours.
opts.coach: A promise you can keep: change comes with a voice in it. That is what turns exposure from threat into a growth conversation.

heads.strong: A team that leans in. The map is on the table and the people who know the tasks best are sorting them with you.
heads.mid: A mixed landing. Some heard opportunity, some heard threat, and the rumor mill got the leftovers.
heads.weak: A quiet meeting and a loud week after. The map became a rumor about cuts before Friday.

reactions.strong: Within two weeks, a team member brings you a task you missed, with their own exposure call attached. The map belongs to the team now, and Tuesday's task sort gives each of them the same lens for their own week.
reactions.mid: A few people run with it; a few quietly update their resumes. The difference was one promise you did not quite make. Reopen the talk with the freed-hours commitment said out loud.
reactions.weak: The word automated traveled faster than the word redesign. You spend the month rebuilding trust the opening line spent in five minutes.

recap.q: What goes on an AI-exposure map?
opts: The team's recurring tasks, one per line
recap.why: Exposure lives in tasks. People hold portfolios of tasks, and mapping tasks keeps redesign honest while keeping anyone's job off trial.

recap.q: A task blends internal data with judgment calls. Its exposure is most likely...
opts: High: hand it to AI end to end
Partial: AI helps in approved VU tools
Unknowable until a vendor demos it
recap.why: Internal work is yellow-light territory: approved VU tools can draft and summarize while the judgment stays with the person driving.

recap.q: What turns high exposure into something other than a threat?
opts: A redesign the team helps write
recap.why: Change with a voice in it reads as redesign. The commitment that the team helps decide what fills the freed hours is the fear antidote.

recapMsgs.high: Solid grasp of the sort. Now walk your real task list through it.
recapMsgs.mid: Solid. Revisit the sort tells, then build your card.
recapMsgs.low: Take the three sections once more before you map real work.

capstone.headline: Commit to the first pass of your map.
capstone.lead: Commit to the first pass of your team's map. Tasks and roles only, never a name; nothing you type is saved or sent.
capstone.whoLabel: Which slice of your team's work do you map first? Name the task cluster.
capstone.whoPlaceholder: e.g. weekly reporting cycle; intake and scheduling tasks
capstone.practiceLabel: How do you take the first pass?

practices.name: Map it myself first
practices.move: List ten recurring tasks, sort each high, partial, or low, and pressure-test the sort with one trusted peer manager.

practices.name: Map it with the team
practices.move: Bring a blank task list to the next team meeting and build the map together, exposure calls and all.

practices.name: Book the navigator workshop
practices.move: Schedule the navigator-led AI-exposure mapping workshop and arrive with your ten-task list as the raw material.

whens.out: The first pass exists by Friday: ten tasks, each with an exposure call.
The map opens your next team meeting, first item, before status updates.
Map and team conversation both happen within two weeks, booked today.

capstone.evidenceRow: Afterward, one line: which task's exposure call surprised you most?

closing.headline: Take the first pass this week.
closing.lead: Build the map before Friday: ten recurring tasks, each sorted high, partial, or low. This week's Tuesday and Thursday sessions give your team the same lens.

facilitator.audience: Vanderbilt people managers and team leads in the Anchor's Edge weekly rhythm. Works for 6 to 40 on a call; breakouts run in pairs. No prerequisites; April is the Spot AI-Exposed Work month, and this session opens it.
facilitator.pulse: Seven days out, send the pulse: 'Does your ten-task map exist? Which exposure call surprised you? Has the team seen it yet?' Count of completed team maps is the Level 3 metric for the month.

s1.title: The task map
s1.purpose: Install the mapping rule: exposure lives in recurring tasks, never in people or titles.
s1.say: April is about seeing what is changing on your team before it changes you. The instinct is to ask which jobs are safe. McKinsey has studied automation for years and keeps finding that the question is aimed at the wrong unit: machines take over activities, almost never whole jobs. So we start smaller and more honest. What tasks does this team repeat every week?
facilitate: Read the lead, then bring up the In the room card and let it land for a beat.
Run the discussion prompt: one recurring task in task language, name off it. Take two or three voices.
Run the breakout: two recurring tasks in task language, no names attached.

ask.q: What changes when you write down the weekly summary instead of a person's name?
expect: The conversation stops being about someone's job
You can sort it without anyone getting defensive
It gets specific enough to actually redesign
ask.respond: All of it. Task language is what lets you do this month in the open instead of in a locked spreadsheet.

s1.debrief: The map is a list of tasks with rhythms and inputs. People hold portfolios of tasks, and no portfolio is all one color.
s1.watchFor: Managers drifting into naming people or rating roles. Redirect every time: tasks on the map, people in your care.
s1.transition: A list is a start. The sort is where honesty gets tested.
s1.coreNote: Core: skip the breakout; ask for one recurring task in chat instead.

s2.title: The honest sort
s2.purpose: Teach the three exposure calls and their tells, inside the shared traffic light rules.
s2.say: Now sort it straight. High means the task could largely run through AI. Partial means AI helps while a person drives. Low means it stays human. And the sort lives inside the traffic light we share all year: green is public or generic, go; yellow is internal, approved VU tools only; red is private information about people, never.
facilitate: Run Call the exposure live; everyone plays on their own screen.
After the coaching task, pause: ask why it stays human even though AI could draft the words.
Run the breakout: one task, one exposure call, partner challenges it.

ask.q: Which pull is stronger in your own sort: calling everything exposed, or calling nothing exposed?
expect: Panic sorters who see exposure everywhere
Comfort sorters who protect every task
Some will admit they flatter their team's work
ask.respond: Both pulls are fear in different clothes. The honest sort is the kind thing; it is what makes the redesign real instead of cosmetic.

s2.debrief: Repetitive and rule-based leans high. Judgment over internal work leans partial, in approved VU tools. Trust and private people data stay human, always.
s2.watchFor: Anyone suggesting AI for red-light work like coaching notes or performance concerns. Restate the light: private information about people, never.
s2.transition: You have a sorted map. Now it has to survive contact with the team.
s2.coreNote: Core: run the trainer, skip the breakout, take one voice on the debrief question.

s3.title: The team talk
s3.purpose: Equip managers to open the exposure conversation as invitation and redesign, with a keepable promise.
s3.say: Your team will hear about AI exposure from somewhere: a headline, a rumor, or you. The version they hear from you can come with tasks on the table and a promise you can keep, which is that the people who do the work help decide what fills the freed hours. We are going to build that opening.
facilitate: Run Open the team conversation; give the room two minutes for both choices.
Ask one volunteer to read a weak outcome aloud; let the room name what went wrong.
Point at the pattern: task map on the table, redesign promise out loud.

ask.q: Why is 'nobody's job changes' the wrong promise even though it feels kind?
expect: Work will change, so the promise breaks
It spends credibility you will need later
The team hears a manager who has not looked closely
ask.respond: Right. Promise the thing you control: change arrives as redesign, with their voice in it. That one holds.

s3.debrief: The strong open has a shape: here is our task map, here is my honest sort, help me decide what the freed hours become.
s3.watchFor: Managers rehearsing reassurance instead of invitation. Push them toward the ask: what is your read on this map?
s3.transition: Quick recap, then your own map goes on a card.
s3.coreNote: Core: everyone runs the builder solo; skip the read-aloud.

facilitator.capstoneSay: Now commit to the first pass. Pick the slice of your team's work you map first, choose how you take the pass, pick the window, and copy the card somewhere you will see it before Friday. Tasks and roles only, never a name. Two minutes, quiet, go.
facilitator.closeSay: You leave with a lens and a map to build. Tomorrow's Take-Off Tuesday hands every member of your team the same skill at the task level: automate, augment, or leave alone, one task at a time. Thursday's Thrive Thursday sharpens the critical thinking that keeps the whole month honest, sorting AI hype from real value. If you want to go deeper, the LinkedIn Learning course AI for Leaders by Doug Rose pairs with the navigator-led mapping workshop.

contingencies.if: Screen share or the site fails mid-session
contingencies.then: Paste the learner link in chat and narrate from your own browser; every interaction runs on learner devices without the share.
Run the breakout prompts as 60-second chat storms: everyone types their answer at once, you read the best three aloud.

contingencies.if: A manager names a specific employee while sorting a task
contingencies.then: Protect them warmly and immediately: 'Hold that. Tasks and roles, never names.' Exposure belongs to work, and the norm only holds if you hold it every time.

contingencies.if: The room turns anxious about their own manager roles
contingencies.then: Name it honestly: manager work is heavy with low-exposure tasks like coaching and judgment calls, and the mapping skill itself is exactly the kind of work that stays valuable.

toughQuestions.q: Isn't this just building the case for cutting my team?
toughQuestions.a: The map is a redesign tool, and Goal 3 is workforce readiness: freed hours moving to higher-value work, skills growing before the change arrives. A team that sorts its own work shapes what comes next; a team that waits gets sorted by someone else's spreadsheet.

toughQuestions.q: What if a task sorts as high exposure but the approved tools can't do it yet?
toughQuestions.a: Then the map is ahead of the tooling, which is the good direction. Log the task, note what the tool would need, and revisit quarterly. High exposure is a signal about the shape of the work, and the redesign can start before the automation does.

toughQuestions.q: Should I share the map with HR or leadership?
toughQuestions.a: Share the task-level map, yes; that is exactly the insight Goal 3 asks managers to surface. Keep it in task language with no names attached, and pair every high-exposure call with your redesign intent so it reads as a plan, never as a cut list.

templates.title: Pre-work invite (paste into the calendar invite)
templates.body: Subject: Monday, 45 minutes on seeing AI-exposed work before it changes your team. Bring a rough sense of the five tasks your team repeats every week. No prep documents, no names. Live and interactive; have the session link open on your own screen.

templates.title: 7-day pulse (send one week after)
templates.body: Subject: Does the map exist? Three lines, reply whenever: 1) Does your ten-task map exist, with exposure calls? 2) Which call surprised you? 3) Has the team seen it, and what did they add?
